items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    In the heavy-fermion metal
                    <a:math xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <a:mrow>
                        <a:mrow>
                          <a:msub>
                            <a:mrow>
                              <a:mi>YbRh</a:mi>
                            </a:mrow>
                            <a:mrow>
                              <a:mn>2</a:mn>
                            </a:mrow>
                          </a:msub>
                        </a:mrow>
                        <a:mrow>
                          <a:msub>
                            <a:mrow>
                              <a:mi>Si</a:mi>
                            </a:mrow>
                            <a:mrow>
                              <a:mn>2</a:mn>
                            </a:mrow>
                          </a:msub>
                        </a:mrow>
                      </a:mrow>
                    </a:math>
                    , quantum criticality at a suppressed antiferromagnetic order is governed by the interplay of local magnetic moments and itinerant conduction electrons. We demonstrate how this can be investigated by a new experimental approach that enables the observation of electron spin resonance (ESR) across a broad range of frequencies and fields at very low temperatures. This allowed us to cover a large part of the phase diagram from the paramagnetic Fermi-liquid phase to the phase with antiferromagnetic order and including the quantum-critical regime. Both the ESR
                    <c:math xmlns:c="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <c:mi>g</c:mi>
                    </c:math>
                    factor and the linewidth present distinct behaviors in these three regimes, providing further insight into the physics across a quantum critical point. Notably, when cooling down at a field directly toward the quantum critical point, both
                    <e:math xmlns:e="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <e:mi>g</e:mi>
                    </e:math>
                    factor and linewidth continuously decrease. Furthermore, we observe a very good matching of the
                    <g:math xmlns:g="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <g:mi>g</g:mi>
                    </g:math>
                    -factor behavior upon field tuning and temperature tuning toward the quantum-critical point. We analyze and discuss the results in the context of present theories on ESR in strongly correlated electron systems.
                  </jats:p>
title: Evolution of Electron Spin Resonance through a Metallic Quantum Critical Phase Diagram

<jats:p>
                    This Letter presents a combination of searches for Higgs boson pair (
                    <a:math xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <a:mi>H</a:mi>
                      <a:mi>H</a:mi>
                    </a:math>
                    ) production performed by the ATLAS and CMS Collaborations using proton-proton collision datasets recorded at
                    <c:math xmlns:c="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <c:msqrt>
                        <c:mi>s</c:mi>
                      </c:msqrt>
                      <c:mo>=</c:mo>
                      <c:mn>13</c:mn>
                      <c:mtext> </c:mtext>
                      <c:mtext> </c:mtext>
                      <c:mi>TeV</c:mi>
                    </c:math>
                    during the Large Hadron Collider Run 2, corresponding to integrated luminosities ranging between 126 and
                    <e:math xmlns:e="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <e:mn>140</e:mn>
                      <e:mtext> </e:mtext>
                      <e:mtext> </e:mtext>
                      <e:msup>
                        <e:mi>fb</e:mi>
                        <e:mrow>
                          <e:mo>−</e:mo>
                          <e:mn>1</e:mn>
                        </e:mrow>
                      </e:msup>
                    </e:math>
                    . The upper limit at the 95% confidence level on the total
                    <g:math xmlns:g="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <g:mi>H</g:mi>
                      <g:mi>H</g:mi>
                    </g:math>
                    signal strength, defined as the ratio of the measured cross section to the standard model (SM) prediction, corresponds to 2.5, with an expected value of 1.7 (2.8) assuming the absence (presence) of the SM
                    <i:math xmlns:i="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <i:mi>H</i:mi>
                      <i:mi>H</i:mi>
                    </i:math>
                    signal. The strength of the
                    <k:math xmlns:k="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <k:mi>H</k:mi>
                      <k:mi>H</k:mi>
                    </k:math>
                    signal is measured to be
                    <m:math xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <m:msubsup>
                        <m:mn>0.8</m:mn>
                        <m:mrow>
                          <m:mo>−</m:mo>
                          <m:mn>0.7</m:mn>
                        </m:mrow>
                        <m:mrow>
                          <m:mo>+</m:mo>
                          <m:mn>0.9</m:mn>
                        </m:mrow>
                      </m:msubsup>
                    </m:math>
                    relative to the SM prediction. The observed significance is found to be 1.1 standard deviations whereas 1.3 are expected for the SM
                    <o:math xmlns:o="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <o:mi>H</o:mi>
                      <o:mi>H</o:mi>
                    </o:math>
                    signal. Constraints are set on the Higgs boson trilinear self-coupling and on the couplings of two Higgs bosons to two vector bosons, both normalized to the SM predictions and denoted as
                    <q:math xmlns:q="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <q:msub>
                        <q:mi>κ</q:mi>
                        <q:mi>λ</q:mi>
                      </q:msub>
                    </q:math>
                    and
                    <s:math xmlns:s="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <s:msub>
                        <s:mi>κ</s:mi>
                        <s:mrow>
                          <s:mn>2</s:mn>
                          <s:mi>V</s:mi>
                        </s:mrow>
                      </s:msub>
                    </s:math>
                    , respectively. The observed individual constraints at the 95% confidence level are
                    <u:math xmlns:u="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <u:mrow>
                        <u:mo>−</u:mo>
                        <u:mn>0.71</u:mn>
                        <u:mo><</u:mo>
                        <u:msub>
                          <u:mrow>
                            <u:mi>κ</u:mi>
                          </u:mrow>
                          <u:mrow>
                            <u:mi>λ</u:mi>
                          </u:mrow>
                        </u:msub>
                        <u:mo><</u:mo>
                        <u:mn>6.1</u:mn>
                      </u:mrow>
                    </u:math>
                    and
                    <w:math xmlns:w="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <w:mn>0.73</w:mn>
                      <w:mo><</w:mo>
                      <w:msub>
                        <w:mi>κ</w:mi>
                        <w:mrow>
                          <w:mn>2</w:mn>
                          <w:mi>V</w:mi>
                        </w:mrow>
                      </w:msub>
                      <w:mo><</w:mo>
                      <w:mn>1.3</w:mn>
                    </w:math>
                    , while the expected constraints assuming the presence of the SM
                    <y:math xmlns:y="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <y:mi>H</y:mi>
                      <y:mi>H</y:mi>
                    </y:math>
                    signal are
                    <ab:math xmlns:ab="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <ab:mo>−</ab:mo>
                      <ab:mn>1.3</ab:mn>
                      <ab:mo><</ab:mo>
                      <ab:msub>
                        <ab:mi>κ</ab:mi>
                        <ab:mi>λ</ab:mi>
                      </ab:msub>
                      <ab:mo><</ab:mo>
                      <ab:mn>6.7</ab:mn>
                    </ab:math>
                    and
                    <cb:math xmlns:cb="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <cb:mn>0.66</cb:mn>
                      <cb:mo><</cb:mo>
                      <cb:msub>
                        <cb:mi>κ</cb:mi>
                        <cb:mrow>
                          <cb:mn>2</cb:mn>
                          <cb:mi>V</cb:mi>
                        </cb:mrow>
                      </cb:msub>
                      <cb:mo><</cb:mo>
                      <cb:mn>1.4</cb:mn>
                    </cb:math>
                    .
                  </jats:p>
title:
Combination of ATLAS and CMS Searches for Higgs Boson Pair Production at
